title: Transcranial Photobiomodulation Attenuates Neurogenic Inflammation and Sensory Hypersensitivity in a Nitroglycerin-Induced Migraine Model: Toward a Nonpharmacological Therapy.
first_affiliation: Neurosciences Research Center, Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Tabriz, Iran, tbzmed.ac.ir.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Migraine is a debilitating neurological condition, characterized by headache, photophobia, and heightened mechanical/thermal sensitivity. Current pharmacological therapies often lead to incomplete relief and adverse effects, necessitating the use of noninvasive alternatives. This study evaluated transcranial photobiomodulation (PBM) in a nitroglycerin (NTG)-induced migraine model in male mice.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Mice were assigned to Sham, NTG, NTG + Sumatriptan (SUMA; 600 µg/kg, s.c.), NTG + PBM, and NTG + PBM + SUMA groups. Over 9 days, NTG (5 mg/kg) was injected intraperitoneally every other day to develop an animal model of chronic migraine. The PBM protocol involved daily irradiation (810 nm) on the occipital bone of the head for 5 s over 9 days. The animals underwent behavioral testing for photophobia, mechanical allodynia, and thermal sensitivity. The trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC) was assessed for miR-155 expression by real-time PCR and protein expression of phospho-NF-κB, IL-1β, transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) and vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), c-Fos, and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) using immunoblotting.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Behavioral assessment revealed that PBM significantly reduced head scratching and improved exploratory activity, decreased light aversion, reversed periorbital/hindpaw mechanical allodynia, and prolonged thermal withdrawal latency compared to the NTG group. Moreover, PBM downregulated miR-155 expression and decreased levels of inflammatory mediators and migraine-associated neuropeptides in the TNC. Notably, combined PBM and SUMA treatment resulted in improvements in behavioral and molecular outcomes compared to either treatment alone.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: These results indicate that PBM inhibited migraine-like behaviors and decreased the expression of numerous molecular markers that are linked to neuroinflammation and trigeminal activation in the TNC. These findings establish a foundation for additional research on transcranial PBM as a noninvasive method for modulating migraine-related behavioral responses.

title: Umbrella review of low-level light therapy: evidence across clinical conditions.
first_affiliation: Global Cooperation Center, Korea Institute of Oriental Medicine, Daejeon, Korea, Republic of.

abstract.text: Low-level light therapy (LLLT) and photobiomodulation (PBM) have been studied in diverse clinical fields. Although numerous systematic reviews have been published, their findings are fragmented and inconsistent. This umbrella review of systematic reviews aimed to synthesize the evidence on the effectiveness and safety of LLLT across various clinical conditions. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science databases were searched from inception to February 24, 2026. Eligible studies were systematic reviews or meta-analyses of LLLT in humans. Data on clinical conditions, intervention characteristics, overall direction of conclusions, and adverse events were extracted. Methodological quality was assessed using AMSTAR 2. A total of 100 systematic reviews were included, representing 1,164 primary-study occurrences and 790 unique eligible primary studies. Oral and dental conditions accounted for the largest evidence base (53 reviews), followed by musculoskeletal disorders (22 reviews), oncology-related complications (8 reviews), and wound and lymphatic conditions (8 reviews). Overall, 62 reviews reached conclusions favoring the evaluated intervention, 34 reported neutral or mixed conclusions, and 4 had unclear conclusions. The highest proportion of favorable conclusions was observed for oncology-related complications. Of the 100 reviews, 11 reported one or more adverse events or side effects, 32 explicitly reported no adverse events, and 57 did not provide adverse-event information. Most reviews received low (30.0%) or critically low (60.0%) overall confidence ratings using AMSTAR 2. The review literature suggests potential clinical benefit of LLLT in selected indications, particularly oncology-related complications such as oral mucositis. However, these descriptive patterns do not establish treatment efficacy or the certainty of the underlying evidence. Heterogeneity in treatment parameters, generally low methodological confidence, and incomplete adverse-event reporting limit interpretation and preclude firm conclusions about safety.

title: Photobiomodulation therapy versus sham for tibial and metatarsal bone stress injuries in military trainees: A randomized controlled trial.
first_affiliation: Department of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, F. Edward Hébert School of Medicine, Uniformed Services University, Bethesda, MD, 20814, United States; Department of Rehabilitation Medicine, Brooke Army Medical Center, San Antonio, TX, United States; The Geneva Foundation, 950 Broadway, Suite 307, Tacoma, WA, 98402, United States. Electronic address: daniel.rhon@usuhs.edu.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To compare the effectiveness of active versus sham photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) on time to graduation and bone healing in military trainees with lower extremity bone-stress injuries (BSI).

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: Participants were trainees at the Medical Education and Training Campus, San Antonio, Texas, with MRI-confirmed metatarsal and/or tibial BSI, enrolled between June 2023 and November 2024. All participants received standard-of-care treatment and were randomized to active or sham PBMT. The primary outcome was time to graduation (days), analyzed with a cause-specific Cox model. Secondary outcomes, assessed at four months, were on-time graduation (yes/no), the Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale (DVPRS), the Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS), and bone healing on MRI.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: 103 participants were randomized; 97 included in the final analysis. The mean age (SD) was 23.7 (4.2) years, 52.6% female. Both extremities were affected in 47.4% of the cohort; the tibia in 70.1% and a metatarsal in 28.9% (1.0% both), with BSI severity ranging from Fredericson grade I to IVb. Only 37.1% of participants graduated on time. Time to graduation did not differ between treatment groups (Hazard Ratio for Sham versus Treatment 0.95; 95%CI 0.61 to 1.48; p = 0.83) nor did on-time graduation (Risk Ratio 0.91; 95%CI 0.54 to 1.52; p = 0.71) or BSI healing on MRI (Risk Ratio 0.89; 95%CI 0.68 to 1.16; p = 0.54). Furthermore, sex, laterality, and BSI location did not predict successful on-time graduation. Pain (mean difference [95%CI] -0.74 [-2.31 to 0.83]; p = 0.84) and function (5.95 [-7.92 to 19.81]; p = 0.89) were not significantly different at 4 months.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Time to graduation, bone healing, pain intensity, and physical function did not differ significantly between trainees with BSI who received PBMT versus sham. Given the substantial resource investment, these results should be weighed when considering routine use of PBMT to manage BSIs in this setting.

abstract.label: TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: ClinicalTrials.gov # NCT05843864.

title: Photobiomodulation therapy combined with a static magnetic field in critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation: protocol for a multicentre randomised triple-blind placebo-controlled trial.
first_affiliation: Laboratory of Phototherapy and Innovative Technologies in Health (LaPIT), Post-graduate Program in Rehabilitation Sciences, Nove de Julho University, São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil ernesto.leal.junior@gmail.com.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Ventilator-induced diaphragmatic dysfunction is a common complication in critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation and is associated with prolonged ventilatory support, delayed weaning and increased length of stay in the intensive care unit (ICU). Strategies that preserve respiratory muscle function may therefore improve recovery in this population. Photobiomodulation therapy combined with a static magnetic field (PBMT-sMF) has been proposed as a non-invasive intervention capable of modulating biological processes involved in muscle function. However, high-quality evidence in mechanically ventilated ICU patients remains limited.

abstract.label: METHODS AND ANALYSIS
abstract.text: This is a multicentre, randomised, triple-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Critically ill patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation will be randomly allocated to receive PBMT-sMF or placebo. The intervention will be applied once daily to predefined anatomical sites over the respiratory muscles during ICU stay. The primary outcome is ICU length of stay, defined as days from ICU admission to ICU discharge. Secondary outcomes include diaphragm thickness by ultrasonography, time to successful weaning from mechanical ventilation, hospital length of stay and selected physiological and laboratory parameters. Data will be analysed using appropriate statistical methods.

abstract.label: ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION
abstract.text: Ethics approval has been obtained by the Research Ethics Committee of the coordinating institution Associação Dr. Bartholomeu Tacchini (approval number: 7.525.651). Informed consent will be obtained from legally authorised representatives and from participants if capacity is regained. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and scientific conferences.

title: Photobiomodulation-Mediated Modulation of TGF-β/Smad Signaling in Stem Cell-Driven Osteogenesis.
first_affiliation: Laser Research Centre, Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Johannesburg, Doornfontein, South Africa.

abstract.text: Bone regeneration remains a significant clinical challenge as a result of limitations presented by autografts, allografts, and synthetic implants. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) serve as key drivers of osteogenesis as they can differentiate into osteoblasts and osteocytes. This process is, however, regulated by the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling pathway, which can upregulate the Runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2) to promote early proliferation and commitment through canonical Smad signaling, and also inhibit late-stage differentiation to prevent excessive matrix deposition. These responses are refined further by noncanonical pathways. Photobiomodulation (PBM), a noninvasive light-based therapy, has emerged as a promising modulator of stem cell-driven osteogenesis, as it can interact with the TGF-β/Smad pathway. PBM exerts effects on the mitochondria, activating cytochrome c oxidase, increasing ATP production, and generating reactive oxygen species in a controlled manner. This leads to a stimulation of MSC proliferation, migration, and osteogenic differentiation. Emerging evidence from various studies shows that PBM can also modulate TGF-β/Smad signaling by activating latent TGF-β, enhancing Smad phosphorylation, and modulating the noncanonical pathways. However, evidence examining this interaction specifically during MSC osteogenesis are few, and the mechanisms underlying their interaction are incompletely understood. This review, therefore, critically examines existing evidence to elucidate some of these mechanisms for MSC osteogenesis. Although it is promising, challenges still exist in standardizing PBM parameters and conducting targeted studies in clinically relevant three-dimensional models. A clearer understanding of these interactions could provide a basis for future research aimed at advancing noninvasive regenerative strategies for bone defects and osteoporosis.

title: Wavelength dependent effects of red and infrared photobiomodulation on neuropathic pain, skeletal muscle integrity, and mitochondrial respiration.
first_affiliation: Laboratory of Neuroanatomy Functional of Pain, Department of Anatomy, Institute of Biomedical Science, Universidade de Sao Paulo, Sao Paulo, Brazil.

abstract.text: Neuropathic pain is a chronic and difficult to treat condition affecting up to 10% of the population, significantly impairing quality of life and representing a public health concern. Photobiomodulation (PBMT) has emerged as a promising therapeutic approach, as photons can reach mitochondria and promote beneficial effects, including increased ATP production, reduced oxidative stress and inflammation, and improved mitochondrial metabolism and regeneration. However, gaps remain regarding its effects on mitochondrial dynamics in neuropathic pain. This study investigated the impact of PBMT at two wavelengths (660 nm, red and 904 nm, infrared) on nociceptive behavior (tactile allodynia, mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia), histological alterations, mitochondrial respiration, and protein expression by Western blotting in an experimental neuropathic pain model in male Wistar rats. PBMT reduced mechanical hyperalgesia and tactile allodynia, decreased inflammatory features, and promoted hyporadiance detected by infrared thermography. Chronic constriction of the sciatic nerve significantly reduced mitochondrial respiration in the gastrocnemius muscle. Although PBMT did not restore mitochondrial respiratory capacity, it induced relevant molecular alterations in mitochondrial proteins. Specifically, PBMT increased the expression of OPA1, a key regulator of mitochondrial dynamics, and modulated components of the electron transport chain and ATP synthase in a wavelength-dependent manner. Overall, PBMT modulated nociception and promoted mitochondrial molecular adaptations. These findings suggest that PBMT-induced analgesia may involve mechanisms independent of skeletal muscle mitochondrial bioenergetic restoration. Distinct wavelength-dependent responses further contribute to therapeutic parameter optimization and support future translational and clinical research. Clinical trial number: not applicable.

title: Photobiomodulation therapy and Wnt/β-catenin signaling in periodontal ligament stem cells during orthodontic tooth movement: A hypothesis and literature review.
first_affiliation: Department of Orthodontics, School of Dentistry, Iran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran. Electronic address: bahramirashin@yahoo.com.

abstract.text: Orthodontic treatment usually takes 18 to 36 months that can lead to time-dependent side effects (like caries and root resorption). Hence, there is growing interest in safely accelerating orthodontic tooth movement (OTM). Photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) has been proposed as a non-invasive approach to accelerate OTM, but clinical findings are inconsistent. Discrepancies may be due to irradiation protocols (light source, wavelength, energy density, exposure time), the orthodontic stage at which PBMT is applied, and the appliance used. A common component across these settings is the periodontal ligament stem cell (PDLSC). PDLSCs are mechanosensitive progenitor cells that contribute to the stress-strain response underlying OTM, and canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling is a key, but not the sole, regulator that balances OPG- and RANKL-mediated bone resorption against osteogenic bone formation; inflammatory mediators, non-coding RNAs, epigenetic mechanisms, and patient-related factors also regulate periodontal remodeling. In vitro studies indicate that PBMT affects PDLSC proliferation, osteogenic differentiation, and RANKL/OPG expression; only one preliminary study, in unloaded cells and at transcript level, suggests that it may upregulate Wnt/β-catenin and TGF-β pathway components. On this basis, we propose a hypothetical framework in which PBMT-related mitochondrial and redox signaling might intersect with force-induced Wnt activation, with each link graded by level of evidence. This framework is unconfirmed: no study has combined orthodontic-like loading, characterized PDLSCs, and multi-level assessment of Wnt/β-catenin signaling under PBMT, and faster movement should not be assumed advantageous without periodontal safety data. Mechanistic and in vivo studies, including inhibition experiments, are needed.

title: Photobiomodulation therapy has a negligible effect as an adjunct to motor control exercise in people with chronic non-specific low back pain: a randomised trial.
first_affiliation: Department of Global Public Health and Primary Care, University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway; Laboratory of Phototherapy and Innovative Technologies in Health (LaPIT), Post-Graduate Program in Rehabilitation Sciences, Universidade Nove de Julho, São Paulo, Brazil. Electronic address: shaiane.tomazoni@gmail.com.

abstract.label: QUESTION
abstract.text: In adults with chronic non-specific low back pain, does adding photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) to a program of motor control exercise (MCE) improve pain intensity, disability and circulating prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) concentrations compared with sham PBMT plus MCE?

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: A randomised controlled trial was conducted with concealed allocation, intention-to-treat analysis and blinding of participants, therapists and assessors.

abstract.label: PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: Adults aged 18 to 65 years seeking treatment for chronic non-specific low back pain of ≥ 3 months in duration.

abstract.label: INTERVENTION
abstract.text: Participants were randomly allocated to active PBMT plus MCE or sham PBMT plus MCE. Both groups received 12 treatment sessions over 6 weeks.

abstract.label: OUTCOME MEASURES
abstract.text: Assessments were completed at baseline and 6 weeks, with follow-up assessments at 1 month after the end of the intervention period and at 3, 6 and 12 months after randomisation. Primary outcomes were pain intensity (0 to 10 numerical rating scale) and disability (0 to 24 Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire) at 6 weeks, in which higher scores indicated greater severity. Secondary outcomes were: pain and disability at follow-up timepoints; circulating PGE2 concentrations at 6 weeks; and medication use, concomitant care and adverse events throughout the follow-up period.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 148 participants were randomised (74 per group). The intention-to-treat analysis showed that PBMT plus MCE had a negligible effect compared with sham plus MCE at 6 weeks for pain intensity (MD -0.4 points, 95% CI -1.2 to 0.4), disability (MD -0.7 points, 95% CI -2.4 to 0.9) or circulating PGE2 concentrations (MD 31 pg/ml, 95% CI -4 to 66). Negligible between-group differences were observed throughout the 12-month follow-up period, and no treatment-related adverse events occurred.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Adding PBMT to MCE did not provide clinically important additional improvements in pain intensity, disability or circulating PGE2 concentrations compared with sham plus the same exercise program.

title: Postburn Cubital Tunnel Syndrome Electrophysiological and Functional Responses to High-Intensity Laser Therapy Versus Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
journal: Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation
first_affiliation: Department of Physical Therapy for Integumentary, Faculty of Physical Therapy, Benha University, Benha, Egypt; Department of Physical Therapy for Surgery, Faculty of Physical Therapy, Ahram Canadian University, Giza, Egypt. Electronic address: mahmoud.mohamed@fpt.bu.edu.eg.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To compare the additional effects of high-intensity laser therapy (HILT) and extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT), combined with ulnar nerve gliding exercises (UNGE), on electrophysiological and functional outcomes in patients with postburn cubital tunnel syndrome (CuTS).

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Prospective assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomized controlled trial.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: University outpatient rehabilitation clinic.

abstract.label: PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: Participants with postburn CuTS involving the upper extremity (N=75).

abstract.label: INTERVENTIONS
abstract.text: Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to HILT+UNGE (n=25), ESWT+UNGE (n=25), or UNGE alone (n=25) for 4 weeks.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
abstract.text: Primary outcomes were ulnar motor nerve conduction velocity (MNCV) across the elbow and compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes recorded from the abductor digiti minimi during ulnar nerve stimulation at 3 standardized sites. The secondary outcome was the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) score. Assessments were performed at baseline, posttreatment, and 12-week follow-up.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: All participants completed the intervention, and 69 completed the 12-week follow-up. Significant posttreatment versus pretreatment changes were observed for MNCV, CMAP amplitudes, and DASH scores (all P<.001). Both HILT and ESWT produced greater improvements than UNGE alone at posttreatment and follow-up (all P<.001). HILT resulted in significantly greater improvements than ESWT across all electrophysiological outcomes and DASH scores. No intervention-related adverse events were reported.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Both HILT and ESWT combined with UNGE improved nerve conduction and upper-limb function more than UNGE alone in patients with postburn CuTS. HILT produced superior electrophysiological and functional outcomes compared with ESWT, with benefits maintained at 12-week follow-up.

title: Light stimuli attenuates inflammatory activation in primary bone marrow-derived macrophages.
journal: Photochemical & photobiological sciences : Official journal of the European Photochemistry Association and the European Society for Photobiology
first_affiliation: Bone Research Lab, Ribeirao Preto School of Dentistry, University of Sao Paulo, Café Avenue, Ribeirao Preto, SP, 14040-090, Brazil.

abstract.text: Bone repair depends on a regulated macrophage-driven inflammatory response. Non-activated macrophages (M0) differentiate into pro-inflammatory (M1) or anti-inflammatory (M2) phenotypes in response to microenvironmental signals. This study evaluated, in vitro, the effects of photobiomodulation (PBM) on bone marrow-derived macrophage polarisation. Monocytes were isolated, differentiated into macrophages (M0), and induced to acquire M1- or M2-associated characteristics. Cells were irradiated using a PBM protocol for bone regeneration (equivalent dose of 2.1 E). Cells were analysed according to morphology, expression of M1 (iNOS, Tnf-α) or M2 markers (Arg1, Cd206), protein expression (iNOS and ARG1), and nitric oxide (NO) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. Statistical analyses of quantitative data were performed using the Mann-Whitney U or Kruskal-Wallis test (p ≤ 0.05). PBM promoted selective and transient modulation of inflammatory and metabolic markers in M0, M1, and M2 macrophages. Compared to non-PBM-treated cells, M1PBM cells had reduced NO levels, increased early ROS levels, and decreased gene and protein expression. In M2PBM cells, transient changes in NO and ROS production were detected, with reduced Cd206 expression and similar Arg1 expression, although increased ARG1 protein expression was detected compared to non-irradiated controls. In M0PBM cells, NO levels remained unchanged, while early ROS levels increased, accompanied by reduced iNos and Arg-1, and increased Cd206 expression. Under the selected parameters, PBM modulated macrophage inflammatory behaviour, but was insufficient to induce classical macrophage polarisation towards a specific phenotype. These findings suggest that modulation of macrophage-mediated inflammatory responses may contribute to the effects of this PBM protocol during bone repair.

title: Effect of Low-Level Laser Therapy on Stability of Dental Implants in D3 and D4 Bone Quality: A Split-Mouth Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial.
journal: The International journal of oral & maxillofacial implants

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Achieving predictable implant stability in low-density maxillary bone (D3-D4) remains clinically challenging because reduced bone density is associated with greater early loss of stability and an increased risk of implant failure. Photobiomodulation (PBM) has been proposed to enhance osseointegration; however, clinical evidence regarding its effect on implant stability in low-density bone remains limited and inconsistent. The aim of this study is to evaluate the effect of 940-nm diode laser photobiomodulation (PBM) on implant stability during early healing in low-density maxillary bone (D3-D4).

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: This split-mouth, randomized controlled clinical trial included medically healthy adults who required bilateral maxillary implants. A total of 40 implants were placed in 10 participants using a guided flapless protocol. Test sites received 940-nm diode laser PBM immediately after implant placement and at 2-week intervals for 2 months, while contralateral sites served as controls. Implant stability was measured using resonance frequency analysis and expressed as implant stability quotient (ISQ) at baseline (T0), 2 months (T1), and 3 months (T2). Data was analyzed using linear mixed-effects model as primary analysis and two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance as supportive.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In the primary mixed-effects analysis, implant stability did not differ significantly between the PBM and control groups at baseline (estimated mean difference [PBM control], -2.45 ISQ; P = 0.341). At 2 months, PBM-treated implants demonstrated significantly higher estimated stability than control implants (mean difference, 6.30 ISQ; 95% CI, 1.21-11.39; P = 0.016). At 3 months, no significant between-group difference was observed (mean difference, 0.40 ISQ; P = 0.878). The linear mixed-effects model demonstrated a significant time × treatment interaction (P = 0.042), indicating that implant-stability trajectories differed between the groups over time. The complete-case repeated-measures ANOVA yielded a consistent significant time × treatment interaction (P = 0.007). No adverse effects related to PBM were observed.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Photobiomodulation using a 940-nm diode laser enhanced early implant stability and reduced the magnitude of the stability dip in D3-D4 maxillary bone without affecting final implant stability after 3 months. PBM may represent a safe adjunctive approach to support early osseointegration in low-density bone.

title: 660 nm LED preconditioning programs mitochondrial signaling in BMSCs for functional tracheal cartilage regeneration.
first_affiliation: Department of Thoracic Surgery, Shanghai Pulmonary Hospital, Tongji University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China.

abstract.text: Stem-cell-based cartilage regeneration is limited not only by cell delivery, but also by the difficulty of establishing a stable and functionally competent regenerative cell state before implantation. Here, we report a photonic mitochondrial programming strategy in which 660 nm light-emitting diode (LED) irradiation preconditions bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) to enhance functional tracheal cartilage regeneration. BMSCs were seeded onto egg white-derived ring-shaped porous scaffolds and exposed to defined 660 nm LED irradiation before implantation. Among the tested irradiation conditions, 15 J/cm2 optimally promoted BMSC proliferation, chondrogenic differentiation and cartilage-like extracellular matrix deposition, while suppressing fibrotic, hypertrophic and matrix-degrading phenotypes. Mechanistically, 660 nm LED irradiation enhanced cytochrome c oxidase (CCO) activity, mitochondrial membrane potential, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production and respiratory function, accompanied by moderate reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling. This mitochondrial bioenergetic-redox response activated the PI3K/Akt/mTOR/GSK3β-SOX9 axis, thereby promoting type II collagen, aggrecan and glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix formation. Pharmacological inhibition of ROS signaling, mitochondrial activity, PI3K or mTOR attenuated the LED-induced chondrogenic program. In a rabbit tracheal cartilage ring defect model, 15 J/cm2-preconditioned BMSC-scaffold constructs improved cartilage-like tissue formation, airway epithelial repair, lumen patency and mechanical support after 30 days of observation. These findings support 660 nm LED irradiation as a controllable mitochondrial preconditioning strategy for stem-cell-based functional cartilage regeneration.

title: Photobiomodulation for temporomandibular disorders: A scoping review of laser-parameter reporting in controlled trials.
journal: Cranio : the journal of craniomandibular practice
first_affiliation: Department of Prosthodontics, Government Dental College, Dibrugarh, India.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To map the controlled-trial evidence on photobiomodulation (PBM) for temporomandibular disorders (TMDs), chart the laser dosimetric parameters, quantify reporting completeness, and identify standardization priorities.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Scoping review per JBI methodology, reported per PRISMA-ScR, and registered on the Open Science Framework (project hdz53). PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library (CENTRAL and CDSR), Lens.org, LILACS, and SciELO were searched from inception to July 21 2026. Eligible reports were randomized or non-randomized controlled trials in humans with TMD receiving PBM over the temporomandibular joint or masticatory muscles; reviews, uncontrolled designs, high-intensity or ablative laser, photodynamic therapy, and acupoint-only irradiation were excluded. Records were de-duplicated and screened independently by two reviewers in two stages, with third-reviewer arbitration. Ten dosimetric parameters were charted verbatim, omissions being the primary datum.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 1,733 records, 1,060 were screened after de-duplication and 462 reports were sought; 215 were not retrieved and 247 were assessed at full text. One hundred seventy‑five controlled trials (165 randomized) formed the evidence map, and 167 with an accessible full report were charted; all reporting-completeness proportions are of those 167. Wavelength and session number were reported in 159/167 trials (95%), power density in 20/167 (12%), and total delivered energy in 24/167 (14%). Only 31/167 (19%) reported every element of a minimum reproducibility set, 45/167 (27%) were non-reproducible, and protocols differed substantially within device families.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Controlled trials of PBM for TMD describe the laser incompletely for the delivered dose to be reconstructed. A minimum reporting set, enforced at publication, is a critical step toward reproducible protocols.

title: Emerging therapeutic strategies for medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw: From microenvironmental modulation to precision medicine (Review).
first_affiliation: Department of Stomatology, The Sixth Affiliated Hospital of Jinan University, Jinan University, Dongguan, Guangdong 523000, P.R. China.

abstract.text: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) is a challenging complication associated primarily with antiresorptive and antiangiogenic therapies. Its pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of impaired bone remodeling, angiogenesis, inflammation and infection, immune regulation and soft tissue healing. Established management includes conservative care, antimicrobial and symptomatic treatment when indicated and surgical intervention, however clinical outcomes remain variable. The present review aimed to summarize pharmacological, regenerative, biomaterial-based and physical or adjunctive strategies targeting the pathological microenvironment of MRONJ, with emphasis on their mechanisms of action and clinical evidence. The present review also examines the potential role of precision medicine in individualized risk assessment and treatment. Teriparatide, pentoxifylline/tocopherol, autologous platelet concentrates and human amniotic membrane have varying degrees of clinical support, although evidence remains limited or heterogeneous for several approaches. By contrast, geranylgeraniol, hydrogels, most mesenchymal stromal cell-based or cell-derived strategies, natural products and melatonin are supported predominantly by preclinical or limited clinical evidence. Other adjunctive approaches, including hyperbaric oxygen, ozone therapy, photobiomodulation, laser-assisted surgery and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy, require further validation. Overall, these strategies may complement established management, but their clinical readiness varies. Standardized clinical studies and integration of multidimensional patient data may facilitate more robust evaluation and individualized MRONJ management.

title: Extreme Diagnostic and Therapeutic Heterogeneity Limits Treatment Conclusions in Iliotibial Band Syndrome: A Systematic Review with Level-of-Evidence Stratification.
first_affiliation: Department of Biomedical Sciences, Humanitas University, Pieve Emanuele, Milan, Italy.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS) is a leading cause of lateral knee pain in runners and endurance athletes, yet clinical decision-making remains inconsistent and largely unsupported by high-quality comparative evidence. No comprehensive synthesis has previously integrated all available treatment modalities using a standardized evidence framework, and the evidence base for individual injection-based therapies continues to evolve rapidly.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate all available treatment strategies for ITBS and stratify their efficacy according to the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (CEBM) levels of evidence.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261374567) on 20 April 2026. PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 29 April 2026. Screening, data extraction, and the subsequent review processes were completed by 21 May 2026. An updated search subsequently identified one further eligible trial, published after the original cut-off. Eligible studies included RCTs, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, and case series reporting outcomes in adults with clinically diagnosed ITBS. Studies were classified into five treatment categories: therapeutic exercise, instrumental physical therapy, manual therapy and minimally invasive techniques, injection-based, pharmacological and biologic treatments, and surgical interventions. The primary outcomes were pain reduction and functional improvement; secondary outcomes included return to sport, recurrence, quality of life, patient satisfaction, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool and NIH Quality Assessment Tools.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twenty-four studies involving 1012 patients were included. Improvements in pain and function were reported across all treatment categories. Manual therapy, corticosteroid/pharmacological injections, and platelet-rich plasma reached Level I evidence; therapeutic exercise and instrumental physical therapy Level Ib; surgical treatments Level IV. A single, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trial now provides Level I evidence for ultrasound-guided platelet-rich plasma (PRP) in refractory ITBS, whereas TECAR (Transfer of Energy Capacitive And Resistive), low-level laser, prolotherapy, and hyaluronic acid still lacked any ITBS-specific controlled evidence.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Despite a broad therapeutic landscape, most treatment modalities cannot yet be recommended over one another. Structured rehabilitation remains the reasonable first-line approach for newly diagnosed ITBS. For refractory ITBS, emerging Level I evidence supports ultrasound-guided PRP as a promising, though not yet independently replicated, minimally invasive option; corticosteroid injection, instrumental therapies and surgery may be considered in selected cases. The absence of standardized diagnostic criteria and extreme methodological heterogeneity across studies - rather than limitations of this review - preclude more definitive conclusions. Future research must prioritize diagnostic standardization and rigorous head-to-head comparative trials, including independent replication of the PRP findings.

title: Comparative efficacy of photobiomodulation therapy and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation for temporomandibular disorders: a CONSORT-based methodological appraisal.
first_affiliation: Departament of Dentistry of the Universidade Federal dos Vales do Jequitinhonha e Mucuri (UFVJM), Diamantina, Brazil.

abstract.text: Temporomandibular disorders (TMDs) are among the most common causes of chronic orofacial pain. Although photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT), traditionally referred to as low-level laser therapy (LLLT), and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) are widely used conservative modalities, their comparative efficacy remains uncertain due to inconsistent evidence. This systematic review compared the efficacy of both therapies and critically appraised the reporting quality and selected methodological characteristics of the included clinical studies. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, with the protocol registered in PROSPERO. Clinical trials comparing TENS and PBMT were searched in Medline, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane, and Embase databases using the descriptors "low-level laser therapy," "photobiomodulation," "transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation," and "temporomandibular joint disorders," without restrictions on publication year or language. The reporting quality and selected methodological characteristics of the included studies were critically appraised using a CONSORT-based assessment framework. A total of 402 records were identified, of which 14 met the inclusion criteria, comprising 620 patients with joint pain, muscle pain, and/or disc displacement. A greater number of included studies reported numerically larger improvements in pain relief and maximum jaw opening following PBMT than TENS. However, twelve of the fourteen included studies were classified as Level III, indicating limited reporting quality according to the adapted CONSORT-based methodological appraisal framework. Substantial heterogeneity in diagnostic characteristics, treatment protocols, and outcome assessment limited direct comparisons between interventions. Overall, the available evidence suggests that both PBMT and TENS may improve pain and mandibular function in patients with temporomandibular disorders. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, as the absence of quantitative synthesis and the substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity preclude definitive conclusions regarding the comparative efficacy or superiority of either modality.

title: Photobiomodulation alters base excision repair gene expression in an experimental model of arthritis.
first_affiliation: Departamento de Morfologia, Instituto de Ciências Biológicas, Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora, Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais, Brazil.

abstract.text: Arthritis is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by a metabolic imbalance and oxidative stress, which can lead to significant DNA damage. While photobiomodulation (PBM) is a widely recognized non-invasive therapy for managing arthritic pain and inflammation, its effects on the mechanisms of DNA repair, specifically the Base Excision Repair (BER) pathway, remain unexplored in zymosan-induced arthritis. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of PBM on the mRNA levels of key BER genes in an experimental model of arthritis. Male C57BL/6 mice were subjected to zymosan-induced arthritis and treated with a low-power infrared laser (830 nm; 10 mW, 0.15 and 1.5 J, 15 and 150 s, 0.05 cm2, 200 mW/cm2, 3 or 30 J/cm2, continuous emission mode). Animals were euthanized at 24, 48, and 72 h post-induction, total mRNA was extracted from joint tissues, and transcription of APE1, POLβ, XRCC1, FEN1, and LIG1 genes was quantified using RT-qPCR. Zymosan-induced inflammation significantly altered relative mRNA levels of BER genes over time, generally increasing the expression of XRCC1, FEN1, and LIG1. PBM at 24 h, both 3 and 30 J/cm2 fluences, significantly reduced APE1, FEN1, and LIG1 mRNA levels. At 48 h, PBM reduced XRCC1, FEN1, and LIG1 expression but, at 72 h, PBM increased transcription of LIG1 gene. Transcription of POLβ gene was not significantly affected. These findings suggest that PBM modulates the relative mRNA levels of genes involved in both the short-patch and long-patch BER pathways in zymosan-induced arthritis.

title: Photobiomodulation attenuates BjussuMP-II-induced muscle inflammation: effects on leukocyte recruitment and MIR-223 expression.
journal: Journal of photochemistry and photobiology. B, Biology
first_affiliation: Laboratório de Imunologia Celular Aplicada à Saúde - Fundação Oswaldo Cruz, FIOCRUZ Rondônia, Porto Velho, RO, Brazil.

abstract.text: Bothrops jararacussu is one of the snake species most frequently involved in snakebite envenomation in Brazil. Snake venom metalloproteinases (SVMPs), which account for approximately 26.2% of its venom composition, play a central role in envenomation by inducing hemorrhage, myonecrosis, and a robust local inflammatory response. Although antivenom effectively neutralizes systemic toxicity, its efficacy against local tissue damage remains limited. In this context, the present study investigated the effects of 945 nm LED photobiomodulation on the inflammatory response induced by BjussuMP-II, a PI class SVMP isolated from B. jararacussu venom. Male Swiss mice (18-22 g) were administered BjussuMP-II (50 μg/animal) or PBS (50 μL) intramuscularly into the gastrocnemius muscle. Thirty minutes after BjussuMP-II administration, animals received antivenom, LED photobiomodulation, or combined treatment. Three hours later, histopathological analyses, intravital microscopy, miR-223 expression, and pro-inflammatory cytokine quantification were performed. Antivenom alone showed limited efficacy in controlling the inflammatory response induced by BjussuMP-II. In contrast, photobiomodulation, either alone or combined with antivenom, reduced inflammatory cell infiltration, leukocyte recruitment, leukocyte-endothelium interactions, and IL-6 levels, while modulating miR-223 expression. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that LED photobiomodulation exerts significant immunomodulatory effects on SVMP-induced inflammation and supports its potential as an adjunct to antivenom therapy for mitigating the local manifestations of Bothrops envenomation.

title: Low-power infrared laser on telomere maintenance in an experimental model of arthritis.
journal: Photochemical & photobiological sciences : Official journal of the European Photochemistry Association and the European Society for Photobiology
first_affiliation: Departamento de Morfologia, Instituto de Ciências Biológicas, Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora, Rua José Lourenço Khelmer - s/n, Campus Universitário, São Pedro, Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais, 36036900, Brazil.

abstract.text: Telomere shortening accelerated by inflammation and oxidative stress is a critical factor in arthritic joint degradation. While photobiomodulation (PBM) is known to mitigate inflammation, its impact on nuclear mechanisms governing genomic stability remains poorly understood. This study evaluated the effects of low-power infrared laser on the temporal expression of key telomere maintenance genes (TRF1, TRF2, POT1, and TIN2) in zymosan-induced arthritis. Experimental arthritis was induced via bilateral intra-articular injection of zymosan into the talocrural and subtalar joints of C57BL/6 mice. PBM was initiated 5 h post-induction using a low-power infrared laser (830 nm, 10 mW, 200 mW/cm2, 3 and 30 J/cm2, 0.15 and 1.5 J, 15 and 150 s). Joint tissues were harvested at 24, 48, and 72 h to determine relative mRNA expression levels using RT-qPCR. Zymosan administration alone triggered an acute, compensatory upregulation of all evaluated telomere maintenance genes within 24 h. PBM significantly altered this transcriptional kinetic profile in a time- and fluence-dependent manner. At 24 and 48-hour time points, laser treatment induced a pronounced downregulation of telomere maintenance genes. Conversely, a striking transcriptional rebound occurred at 72 h in the high-fluence group, yielding a highly significant upregulation of TRF2, POT1, and TIN2 relative to untreated arthritic controls. By regulating telomere maintenance kinetics, PBM could prevent replicative senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Mapping this the temporal window, number of laser exposures, and dosing parameters could provide a mechanistic framework for optimizing clinical PBM protocols to preserve genomic stability, extend cellular longevity, and restore tissue homeostasis in arthritic diseases.

title: Knee osteoarthritis management across the joint-preservation continuum: current evidence and future directions.
first_affiliation: Southcoast Health, Dartmouth, MA, United States.

abstract.text: Knee osteoarthritis is a leading cause of chronic pain, disability, and mobility limitation, with increasing prevalence driven by population aging, obesity, and joint injury. Although historically viewed as passive cartilage "wear and tear," knee osteoarthritis is now understood as a heterogeneous whole-joint disease involving cartilage matrix degradation, chondrocyte dysfunction, synovial inflammation, subchondral bone remodeling, genetic and epigenetic susceptibility, and altered biomechanics. This narrative review examines current and emerging strategies for knee osteoarthritis management across the joint-preservation continuum. PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar were searched through August 2026, prioritizing systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, clinical practice guidelines, and relevant primary studies, with selective inclusion of preclinical evidence for emerging therapies. This broader biological understanding has identified therapeutic targets and supports a joint-preservation continuum that extends from weight management, exercise, and pharmacologic symptom control to intra-articular therapies, cartilage restoration, and investigational molecular or gene-based interventions. Currently available intra-articular therapies may provide symptom relief in selected patients but have not demonstrated consistent structural disease modification, and guideline recommendations differ for several intra-articular, orthobiologic, and regenerative treatments because of substantial heterogeneity in the available evidence. Emerging approaches, including cytokine-directed therapy, photobiomodulation, platelet-rich plasma, and tissue engineering, aim to influence disease mechanisms, although their clinical maturity and evidentiary strength vary substantially. Future precision-medicine strategies may integrate clinical phenotype, biological profiles, imaging, biomarkers, and genetic risk to identify patients most likely to progress or respond to specific interventions. At present, no disease-modifying osteoarthritis drug is approved for knee osteoarthritis. Nevertheless, biologically informed, stage-appropriate care may help preserve function, address modifiable disease drivers, and extend native-joint health while maintaining the essential role of total knee arthroplasty for end-stage disease.

title: Photobiomodulation versus ischemic preconditioning for protection against exercise-induced muscle damage: protocol for a randomized controlled trial.
first_affiliation: Southwest Bahia State University, Jequié, BA, Brazil.

abstract.text: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) occurs after unaccustomed eccentric exercise and may impair muscle recovery. Preconditioning with photobiomodulation (PBM) or ischemic preconditioning (IPC) may mitigate EIMD; however, no study has directly compared their effectiveness. This study aims to compare the effects of PBM and IPC applied prior to eccentric exercise on indirect markers of EIMD and associated perceptual responses. We hypothesized that MVIC trajectories would differ among the PBM, IPC, and sham groups, with PBM expected to provide greater preservation of MVIC than IPC. A prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial with concealed allocation, blinded outcome assessors and statistician, and intention-to-treat analysis will be conducted. Healthy men (18-35 years) will be randomly allocated to PBM, IPC, or sham groups (n = 15 per group). After the intervention, participants will perform an eccentric exercise protocol for the elbow flexors consisting of 30 repetitions using a dumbbell load numerically matched to maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) values, with 45-second rest intervals. The primary outcome will be MVIC. Secondary outcomes include rate of force development, delayed-onset muscle soreness, pressure pain threshold, ultrasound echo intensity, range of motion, perceived exertion, and affective responses. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, immediately after exercise (only MVIC), and at 24-, 48-, and 72-hours post-exercise. The primary analysis will assess the group × time interaction on MVIC using linear mixed-effects models, while secondary outcomes will be analyzed exploratorily. This study will provide, to our knowledge, the first direct comparison between PBM and IPC as preconditioning strategies to attenuate EIMD. The findings may help determine the most effective and clinically applicable intervention by considering both physiological and perceptual responses, thereby supporting decision-making in clinical and sports settings.Trial registrationBrazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (REBEC), RBR-6gr5kf; registered February 19, 2020; amended August 26, 2026.

title: Effectiveness of Low-Level and High-level Laser Therapy for Rotator Cuff-Related Shoulder Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
journal: Journal of lasers in medical sciences
first_affiliation: Skin Research Center, Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran.

abstract.text: Introduction: While photobiomodulation and high-power lasers are common for rotator cuff-related shoulder pain, evidence interpretation is hindered by inconsistent dosimetry and clinical findings. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluate the effects of low-level (LLLT) and high-level laser therapy (HLLT) on pain, range of motion (ROM), and shoulder function. Methods: This PROSPERO-registered review included randomized controlled trials comparing LLLT or HLLT against sham, no treatment, or conventional care. Two reviewers independently conducted screening, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Continuous outcomes were synthesized using random-effects models, supplemented by subgroup analyses (LLLT vs. HLLT; laser vs. laser plus exercise) and sensitivity analyses to address heterogeneity. Results: Twenty-three trials (wavelengths 805-1064 nm) were included. Pooled analysis showed that laser therapy significantly reduced overall pain (VAS: MD -5.22; 95% CI -7.56 to -2.88; P<0.001 P<0.001 P<0.001), though improvements in pain at rest, during movement, and at night were not statistically significant. After excluding outliers, modest improvements were noted in active internal rotation (MD 1.14; 95% CI 0.19-2.09; P<0.001 P<0.001 P<0.001) and passive external rotation (MD -1.33; 95% CI -1.92 to -0.73; P<0.001 P<0.001 P<0.001). Subgroup analysis indicated that HLLT yielded superior active-abduction outcomes compared to LLLT (P=0.016 P=0.016 P=0.016). Certainty was limited by heterogeneity, small sample sizes, inconsistent dosimetry, and short follow-up. Conclusion: Laser therapy provides modest, reproducible analgesic benefits, and selective ROM improvements, particularly when HLLT is combined with exercise. Given the limited functional gains and reporting inconsistencies, lasers should be used as an adjunct to structured rehabilitation rather than a standalone treatment. Future trials require standardized dosing and longer follow-ups.

title: Preliminary pre-post changes in neuromuscular performance after application of a wearable photobiomodulation device in young tennis athletes.
first_affiliation: Department of Neurosciences, Biomedicine and Movement, University of Verona, Italy, Department of Human Science and Promotion of Quality of Life, San Raffaele University, Rome.

abstract.text: Athletes require effective recovery strategies to sustain performance, particularly in high-demand sports. Photobiomodulation (PBM) has emerged as a non-invasive approach capable of supporting muscle function without reported adverse effects. Wearable nanotechnology-based devices, such as Taopatch®, allow continuous and localized PBM delivery, representing a potential tool for sports applications. This pilot study investigated the acute effects of Taopatch® on neuromuscular performance in 28 young tennis players (11 females, 17 males; age 14.41 ± 2.60 years). Participants completed Squat Jump (SJ), Counter Movement Jump (CMJ), stiffness, and reaction time assessments before (T1) and after a 15-minute application period (T2). Taopatch® application was associated with pre-post increases in SJ flight time (unadjusted p=0.042) and maximal pre-take-off velocity (Vmax; unadjusted p=0.012), while CMJ concentric work also increased (unadjusted p=0.014). Several effects remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, whereas none remained significant after the more conservative Holm-Bonferroni correction. Stiffness responses varied among subgroups, while reaction time remained unchanged. These preliminary findings suggest a potential association between Taopatch® application and acute changes neuromuscular performance. However, the statistical evidence was sensitive to the multiple-comparison correction applied, and controlled studies are required to confirm these exploratory observations.

title: Effects of Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy, Photobiomodulation, Ultrasound, and Electrotherapy Modalities on Rotator Cuff-Related Shoulder Pain: A Systematic Review.
journal: Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology
first_affiliation: Human Movement Science, Sport and Health, University of Graz, 8010 Graz, Austria.

abstract.text: Background and Objectives: The term rotator cuff-related shoulder pain (RCRSP) refers to pain localized in the deltoid region. RCRSP and the associated pain and functional limitations have a significant impact on the quality of life of those affected. This systematic review aimed to investigate the treatment and follow-up effects of extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT), photobiomodulation (PBM), ultrasound (US), and electrotherapy modalities (ET) in RCRSP. Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted. In addition, the reference lists of the included studies and relevant reviews were screened to identify further eligible studies (snowballing). Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating the treatment and follow-up effects of ESWT, PBM, US, and ET for RCRSP, with control groups receiving sham or alternative physiotherapeutic treatments, were included without restrictions on date or language. Two reviewers independently conducted the literature screening, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment for the included studies. The differences in pain between pre- and post-intervention, the between-group differences (intervention vs. control), as well as subgroups (low-level laser therapy [LLLT] and high-power laser therapy [HPLT]) were analyzed. Results: A total of 20 RCTs with 1153 patients were included. Quality assessment indicated a low risk of bias in 55% of the included studies, some concerns in 35%, and high risk in 10%. In the nature of a sustainable therapy, therapeutic modalities were mostly not applied in isolation but rather in combination with conventional physiotherapeutic interventions. One study showed an end-of-treatment pain reduction for ESWT, and one study showed no follow-up effect on pain. PBM showed a significant but small end-of-treatment effect and an insignificant follow-up effect. The subgroup analysis suggested that only HPLT demonstrated a clear end-of-treatment effect. Due to the limited number of studies, no subgroup analysis could be performed for follow-up outcomes. US showed beneficial small effects both at the end of treatment and at follow-up, while ET demonstrated an end-of-treatment effect. Further studies are needed for the follow-up effect. Conclusions: HPLT, US, and ET showed consistent additive treatment effects, while PBM and US showed follow-up effects. In general, especially for PBM, ESWT, and ET, more studies are needed to gain a broader insight into this topic.

title: Comparison of the Clinical Effectiveness of Two Photobiomodulation Systems for Facial Nerve Dysfunction Following Temporomandibular Joint Surgery.
first_affiliation: Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, Faculty of Dentistry, Ankara University, Ankara, Turkey.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To compare the clinical effectiveness of two photobiomodulation systems for the management of facial nerve dysfunction following temporomandibular joint (TMJ) surgery.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: Twenty-four patients who developed postoperative facial nerve dysfunction after TMJ surgery between May 2022 and April 2026 were randomly assigned to receive photobiomodulation using either the GRR Laser or the SiroLaser Advance Plus system. The treatment began on the first postoperative day and consisted of 15 treatment sessions, administered daily during the first 5 postoperative days and every other day thereafter. Facial nerve function was evaluated on postoperative Days 5, 7, 10, 30, and 60 using the House-Brackmann (HB) grading system, the Sunnybrook Facial Grading System, and the Facial Clinimetric Evaluation (FaCE) Scale.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Both groups showed significant improvements in Sunnybrook and FaCE Scale scores throughout follow-up (both p < 0.001). No significant differences were observed between the groups in House-Brackmann grades at any follow-up time point (all p > 0.05). Linear mixed-effects model analyses demonstrated a significant main effect of time for both Sunnybrook and FaCE Scale scores (both p < 0.001), whereas neither the main effect of group nor the group × time interaction was statistically significant (all p > 0.05). However, change-score analyses from postoperative Day 5 to Day 60 showed significantly greater improvements in Sunnybrook (17.67 ± 3.42 vs. 13.75 ± 6.08; p = 0.036) and FaCE Scale scores (22.92 ± 11.51 vs. 18.64 ± 11.71; p = 0.040) in the GRR Laser group.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Both photobiomodulation systems were associated with progressive improvement in facial nerve function following TMJ surgery. Although change-score analyses showed greater improvements in Sunnybrook and FaCE Scale scores in the GRR Laser group, linear mixed-effects model analyses did not demonstrate a significant difference in the longitudinal recovery pattern between the two treatment groups.

title: Combined photobiomodulation and exosome therapy for muscle and tendon regeneration: an experimental rabbit study.
first_affiliation: Tarbiat Modares University, Tehran, Islamic Republic of Iran.

abstract.text: Achilles tendon injuries are common, especially among athletes, and their treatment remains challenging. Reduced muscle strength and immobility can exacerbate tendon stiffness, leading to disability. This study investigated the effects of adipose tissue-derived mesenchymal stem cell exosomes and low-level laser therapy (LLLT) on muscle and Achilles tendon elasticity in a rabbit model. Twelve New Zealand white rabbits underwent ultrasound imaging of Achilles tendons and gastrocnemius muscles with a 40 MHz probe during flexion and dorsiflexion. Foot stress during movement was measured. To create a partial tendon injury, a 5 mm longitudinal incision, 3 mm deep, was made in the Achilles tendon. Male rabbits were randomly divided into four groups: control, LLLT (830 nm, 15 mW, 3 J/cm²), exosome injection (200 µg/mL), and combined LLLT with exosomes. Treatments were applied on days 1, 8, and 15. Ultrasound evaluations were performed before injury, immediately after, and on days 8 and 21. Tendon and muscle samples were analyzed histologically with hematoxylin-eosin staining. On day 21, the force applied to induce flexion and dorsiflexion of the Achilles tendon and gastrocnemius muscle significantly increased in the combined treatment group compared to the others (P < 0.05). The thickness strain of both muscle and tendon improved significantly with combination therapy (P < 0.05). Histology showed compact, parallel collagen fibers and a well-organized extracellular matrix in tendons treated with LLLT and exosomes. No inflammation was observed, and muscle atrophy was reduced. Combining low-level laser therapy with exosomes derived from ADSCs enhanced the histological, ultrasound-derived, and mechanical aspects related to Achilles tendon repair. This included improvements in tendon and gastrocnemius strain, as well as flexion and dorsiflexion force.

title: Effect of High-Intensity Laser Acupuncture on Muscle Performance, Pain, and Quality of Life in Patients with Chronic Nonspecific Low Back Pain: A Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial [Letter].
first_affiliation: Maharishi Markandeshwar Institute of Physiotherapy and Rehabilitation, Maharishi Markandeshwar (Deemed to be University), Mullana, Ambala, Haryana, India.

title: Effects of Infrared and Dual-Wavelength Photobiomodulation Therapy on Mandibular Bone Healing Following Radiotherapy and Tooth Extraction: An Experimental Study.
journal: Journal of oral pathology & medicine : official publication of the International Association of Oral Pathologists and the American Academy of Oral Pathology
first_affiliation: Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, Faculty of Dentistry, Tokat Gaziosmanpaşa University, Tokat, Turkey.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Osteoradionecrosis (ORN) is a serious complication of head and neck radiotherapy characterized by impaired bone healing. Infrared photobiomodulation therapy (IR-PBMT) and dual-wavelength photobiomodulation therapy (Dual-PBMT) have been proposed as non-invasive approaches to enhance bone regeneration.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Twenty-nine male Wistar-Albino rats were included. An experimental protocol designed to induce mandibular ORN was performed using a single 35 Gy radiation dose followed by mandibular molar extraction. Animals were allocated to four groups: control, radiotherapy plus extraction (RT + EX), RT + EX + IR-PBMT, and RT + EX + Dual-PBMT. IR-PBMT was performed using a 940 nm diode laser, whereas Dual-PBMT combined 632-650 nm red and 904-940 nm infrared wavelengths. Both PBMT protocols were applied extraorally for 14 consecutive days. Bone samples were evaluated histopathologically and immunohistochemically for alkaline phosphatase (ALP), bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2), osteonectin (ONC), and tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The RT + EX group exhibited severe inflammation and tissue destruction, whereas both PBMT-treated groups showed reduced inflammation and partial epithelialization. Osteogenic marker expression was significantly lower and TRAP expression was significantly higher in the RT + EX group than in the control group (p < 0.05). Compared with the RT + EX group, both IR-PBMT and Dual-PBMT significantly increased ALP, BMP-2, and ONC expression and reduced TRAP expression (p < 0.05). ALP expression was significantly higher in the Dual-PBMT group than in the IR-PBMT group, whereas no significant differences between the two protocols were observed for BMP-2, ONC, or TRAP.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Both IR-PBMT and Dual-PBMT improved the evaluated histological and bone-remodeling parameters following radiotherapy and tooth extraction. Because the control animals did not undergo tooth extraction, comparisons with the control group should be interpreted cautiously. Although Dual-PBMT produced a greater increase in ALP expression, the findings do not demonstrate the overall superiority of one PBMT protocol over the other. Both approaches may represent promising adjunctive strategies for mitigating radiation-associated impairment of mandibular bone healing.

title: Photobiomodulation Triggers M1/M2 Macrophage Polarization in Zymosan-Induced Acute Arthritis in Mice.
first_affiliation: Departamento de Morfologia, Instituto de Ciências Biológicas, Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora, Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais, Brazil.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To investigate whether photobiomodulation (PBM) modulates macrophage polarization in zymosan-induced acute joint inflammation, promoting an M1 to M2 phenotype shift.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Mice received intra-articular zymosan and PBM (830 nm, 10 mW) at 3 and 30 J/cm2. Euthanasia occurred at 24, 48, and 72 h. Polarization was assessed via mRNA levels and protein expression.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: At 24 h, both fluences downregulated iNOS and Arg-1 mRNA. The 30 J/cm2 dose sustained steady-state mRNA levels through 72 h. Immunohistochemistry showed that 3 J/cm2 reduced M1 cells at 24 h, while 30 J/cm2 was more effective in promoting M2 polarization at 48 and 72 h. Predominance of M2 over M1 macrophages was observed in all treated groups.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: PBM may modulate acute joint inflammation by driving a phenotypic switch from M1 to M2 macrophages. These regulatory effects depend on irradiation conditions, with higher fluence (30 J/cm2) sustaining a durable pro-resolutive cellular profile.

title: Effectiveness of low-level laser therapy in the rehabilitation of knee meniscus injuries: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
first_affiliation: Department of Physical Therapy and Health Rehabilitation, College of Applied Medical Sciences, Jouf University, Sakaka 72388, Saudi Arabia. hsalserhany@ju.edu.sa.

abstract.text: To evaluate the effectiveness of low-level laser therapy (LLLT) as an adjunct to rehabilitation in reducing pain and improving knee function in adults with MRI-confirmed meniscus injuries. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 40 adults with unilateral meniscus injuries were assigned to either an LLLT group or a placebo group. All participants received a standardized rehabilitation program over six weeks. The primary outcome was pain intensity measured using a visual analogue scale (VAS). Secondary outcomes included knee function (Lysholm score), range of motion (ROM), and physical performance tests. Both groups showed significant improvements; however, the LLLT group demonstrated greater reductions in pain and improvements in function, mobility, and ROM compared with the control group (p < 0.01 for all outcomes). The magnitude of improvement exceeded clinically meaningful thresholds, particularly for pain reduction and functional gains. Adjunctive LLLT was associated with greater improvements in pain and functional outcomes compared with rehabilitation alone. LLLT appears to be a safe and potentially effective complementary modality in the conservative management of meniscal injuries.

title: Effects of Photobiomodulation Therapy on Muscle Strength and Muscle Endurance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
journal: Journal of integrative and complementary medicine
first_affiliation: Beijing Sport University, Beijing, China.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To investigate the effects of photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) on muscle strength and muscle endurance and to explore potential sources of variation related to participant characteristics and intervention parameters.

abstract.label: DATA SOURCES
abstract.text: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, CENTRAL, Scopus, Medline, EBSCOhost, and Web of Science from inception to November 2025.

abstract.label: STUDY SELECTION
abstract.text: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effects of PBMT on muscle performance in healthy humans were selected. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts. Studies were included if they compared PBMT to a placebo control using quantitative outcome measures.

abstract.label: DATA EXTRACTION
abstract.text: Data regarding participant characteristics, intervention protocols, and outcomes were extracted independently by two investigators using a standardized form. Methodological quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool.

abstract.label: DATA SYNTHESIS
abstract.text: Twenty-three RCTs were included and pooled using a random-effects model. PBMT showed small effects on muscle endurance (p = 0.02) and muscle strength (p = 0.04). Subgroup differences were mostly nonsignificant. Muscle endurance benefits were found in athletes (p = 0.05), but not in physically active individuals (p = 0.07). For muscle endurance, favorable parameters included ≤100 mW per diode (p = 0.03), 31-100 J (p = 0.05), a 1-3 min pre-exercise interval (p = 0.03), and ≤4 application sites (p = 0.007). Strength improved with 151-300 J (p = 0.05) and when the interval was over 3 min (p = 0.007).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: PBMT may modestly improve muscle endurance and muscle strength, particularly for endurance-related outcomes. However, subgroup findings remain exploratory, and current evidence is insufficient to define optimal protocols. Further high-quality trials are needed to standardize PBMT parameters for sports performance and rehabilitation.

title: Photobiomodulation for skeletal muscle regeneration: mechanisms, dosimetry, and translational challenges.
first_affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, New York Institute of Technology, New York, NY, United States.

abstract.text: Photobiomodulation (PBM) has gained increasing attention as a non-invasive modality for enhancing skeletal muscle recovery; however, its clinical translation remains limited by inconsistencies in dosimetry, methodology, and reporting across studies. This review synthesizes over two decades of preclinical and clinical research to evaluate how key parameters such as wavelength, irradiance, fluence, pulse structure, and timing affect muscle regeneration. Evidence indicates that red and near-infrared light modulate mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase activity, promoting nitric oxide dissociation, increasing ATP production, and inducing controlled reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling that supports satellite cell activation, angiogenesis, and anti-inflammatory responses. These effects follow a biphasic dose-response relationship and are strongly influenced by tissue optical properties, which differ significantly between animal models and humans, contributing to variability in clinical outcomes. This review highlights critical challenges, including uncertainties in light delivery and tissue-level dose deposition. This review outlines recommendations to improve reproducibility, including standardized dosimetry, radiometric calibration, and integration of PBM with exercise-based rehabilitation. Emerging approaches, such as Monte Carlo light transport modeling and patient-specific optical simulations, are discussed as promising strategies for personalized treatment planning. Collectively, these advances support the transition of PBM from an empirical intervention toward a mechanistically guided and clinically reliable therapy for skeletal muscle regeneration.

title: Comparison of low-level laser therapy and proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation for chronic non-specific neck pain: A randomized controlled trial.
journal: Journal of back and musculoskeletal rehabilitation
first_affiliation: Department of Physiotherapy and Rehabilitation, Faculty of Health Sciences, Istanbul Gedik University, Istanbul, Türkiye.

abstract.text: Background/ObjectivesNon-specific chronic neck pain (NCNP) is a common musculoskeletal disorder associated with pain, disability, and reduced quality of life. The aim of this study was to comparatively evaluate the effects of low-level laser therapy (LLLT) and proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF) on pain severity, pressure pain threshold (PPT), and functionality in individuals diagnosed with NCNP.MethodsIn a three-arm, single-blind randomized controlled trial, 75 participants were randomized. Participants were divided into LLLT (n = 25), PNF (n = 24), and control (n = 26) groups. Conventional treatment was applied in all groups. The primary outcome measure was the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), which assessed pain severity, and the secondary outcome measures were PPT and functionality assessed by the Bournemouth Neck Pain Questionnaire (BNQ). Assessments were performed at the beginning of treatment and at the end of 10 sessions.ResultsSignificant improvements were observed in both the LLLT (p < 0.001) and PNF (p < 0.001) groups compared to the control group in both the primary outcome measure NRS and the secondary outcome measures PPT and BNQ, in both pre- and post-treatment change scores.ConclusionImprovements in pain, pain threshold, and functionality were observed in both the LLLT and PNF groups compared to the control group in NCNP treatment. Neither active treatment method was superior to the other. LLLT and PNF, as non-invasive treatment methods, may be effective and reliable treatment methods for improving pain severity, pain threshold, and functionality in NCNP.

title: Rethinking neurophysiology of delayed onset muscle soreness: updated concepts and mechanisms for mitigation across endurance, resistance, and plyometric exercise.
journal: Frontiers in sports and active living
first_affiliation: Faculty of Sports Science, Ningbo University, Ningbo, China.

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is a physiological response to intense eccentric exercise across endurance, resistance, and plyometric training. Although traditionally attributed primarily to structural muscle damage and inflammation, accumulating evidence indicates that DOMS is a multifactorial neurophysiological response involving complex interactions between peripheral tissue responses, inflammatory signalling, neural sensitisation, proprioceptive alterations, and central nervous system adaptations.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This review aimed to synthesise current evidence on the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying DOMS across endurance, resistance, and plyometric exercise within an integrated neurophysiological framework. It further examined the mechanisms underpinning therapeutic interventions, critically evaluated current approaches to DOMS assessment, and explored their implications for personalised recovery strategies, providing key-take-home to help clinicians and field partitioners.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This systematic review with narrative synthesis followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO). 1,183 articles, including clinical trials examining DOMS neurophysiology and therapeutic interventions across exercise modalities were screened.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The evidence indicates that DOMS cannot be explained by a single biological mechanism. Rather, distinct exercise modalities activate overlapping but different combinations of inflammatory, neural, metabolic, and proprioceptive pathways that influence symptom development and recovery. The findings further indicate that different exercise modalities elicit unique neuromuscular adaptations, with endurance training leading to cumulative inflammatory responses, resistance training inducing nociceptor sensitization, and plyometric exercise disrupting proprioceptive control. Endurance exercise produces IL-6 increase within 48 h but shows inflammation reduction after repeated bouts. Resistance training causes strength loss with Group III/IV nociceptor activation. Plyometric exercise disrupts proprioception alongside C-fiber sensitization. Recovery interventions show DOMS reduction: compression garments SMD = -0.44, acupuncture SMD = -0.89, foam rolling SMD = -0.34, but majority of studies lack extractable effect sizes preventing meta-analysis. Intervention efficacy appeared to vary according to exercise modality, exercise load, and individual neurophysiological responses, suggesting a dose-response influence on recovery outcomes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Collectively, the evidence supports the concept that DOMS should be regarded as a multifactorial neurophysiological response rather than simply a consequence of muscle damage. Exercise-specific recovery optimizes DOMS management: active recovery for endurance, compression/photobiomodulation for resistance, foam rolling/acupuncture for plyometric. Chronic training reduces DOMS through repeated bout adaptation. Future research should prioritise standardised outcome reporting together with mechanistic biomarkers and adequately designed longitudinal studies to strengthen the evidence base. This review highlights the need for individualized and exercise-specific recovery strategies to optimize DOMS mitigation, post-exercise recovery, and requires rehabilitation protocols based on neural and biochemical markers. Recovery interventions should also consider the dose-response relationship between exercise load and neurophysiological stress, as treatment effectiveness may vary according to DOMS severity and training demands. Given the variability in individual responses, integrating multiple assessment tools enhances accuracy and reliability in both research and clinical settings.
